triage.name: Phimosis
triage.reason: A focused genitourinary complaint diagnosed largely by history and inspection of the foreskin, with important distinction from paraphimosis and balanitis.

age.peak: bimodal: infancy/early childhood and older adulthood

demographics: Physiologic phimosis is normal in infancy and early childhood and usually resolves by adolescence
Pathologic phimosis becomes more common with age, especially in uncircumcised older men
Uncircumcised males are affected; circumcised males are essentially spared unless there is scarring at the circumcision line

risk_factors.text: Young age (physiologic phimosis in infants and young boys)
Forceful or premature retraction of the foreskin in childhood

family_history: Lichen sclerosus in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: I can't pull my foreskin back
It hurts when I try to pull the skin back
The tip of my penis gets red and sore
My urine stream is weak and the skin balloons up when I pee

hpi.onset: Gradual; often noticed in infancy or early childhood, or insidiously in adulthood
hpi.duration: Weeks to years; congenital/physiologic cases present from birth
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive tightening of the foreskin opening; may be stable for years then worsen with recurrent inflammation or scarring
hpi.quality: Tight, non-retractile skin; may be painful or painless
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate; severe when urinary obstruction or recurrent infection occurs
hpi.timing: Constant; worse with attempted retraction or erection

associated_symptoms.text: Pain or discomfort with attempted retraction
Redness and inflammation of the glans or foreskin
Ballooning of the foreskin during urination
White scarring or tightening of the foreskin
Discharge or foul odor under the foreskin

pertinent_negatives: Sudden severe pain with a swollen, retracted foreskin

positives.text: Ballooning of the foreskin during urination
Redness of the glans or foreskin
White atrophic scarring of the foreskin

atypical.how_it_differs: Physiologic phimosis is normal; the foreskin is not meant to be retractable in infancy, so presentation is usually parental concern rather than symptoms.
May present with ballooning during urination, recurrent balanitis, or difficulty with hygiene; often discovered during routine care.
More likely to have pathologic phimosis from lichen sclerosus, diabetes, or recurrent infection; may present with urinary obstruction or inability to clean.
Higher risk of recurrent balanoposthitis and more rapid progression due to poor glycemic control and impaired immunity.

general.moderate: Mild discomfort with attempted retraction; otherwise comfortable
general.severe: Ill-appearing, guarding the genital area, reluctant to allow examination
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, diaphoretic, in distress from urinary obstruction or severe infection

findings.maneuver: Gently attempt to retract the foreskin over the glans
findings.finding: Foreskin cannot be retracted to reveal the glans

findings.maneuver: Inspect the foreskin for white, atrophic or sclerotic changes
findings.finding: White, atrophic, sclerotic scarring of the foreskin
Erythema and inflammation of the glans or foreskin

findings.maneuver: Inspect under the foreskin and express the preputial sac

findings.finding: Ballooning of the foreskin during voiding

findings.maneuver: Inspect the position of the foreskin relative to the glans
findings.finding: Foreskin is not retracted behind the glans; no constricting band

findings.maneuver: Inspect the urethral meatus and strip the urethra
Inspect the glans, foreskin and shaft for ulceration

findings.finding: No suprapubic tenderness or palpable bladder

labs.caveat: Pyuria suggests secondary urinary tract infection or balanoposthitis rather than phimosis itself.
Positive nitrite supports a concurrent urinary tract infection, which is uncommon in uncomplicated phimosis.
Elevated only when there is a secondary urinary infection or severe inflammation.
Leukocytosis is not expected in uncomplicated phimosis; it suggests secondary infection such as balanoposthitis or urinary tract infection.
Screen for undiagnosed or poorly controlled diabetes, a strong risk factor for pathologic phimosis and recurrent balanoposthitis.
Helps identify diabetes as the underlying driver of recurrent infection and scarring.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected urethral stricture or obstructive voiding symptoms

findings.text: Narrowed preputial opening with normal urethra

imaging.preferred_when: Children with recurrent urinary infection or suspected obstruction

findings.text: Normal penile anatomy; no mass or abscess

initial.why: Screens for diabetes, a major risk factor for pathologic phimosis
Looks for a secondary urinary tract infection when there are urinary symptoms

supporting.why: Confirms diabetes when glucose is elevated
Evaluates for urethral stricture when obstruction is suspected
supporting.only_if: weak stream, ballooning, or retention persists after treating phimosis

supporting.why: Assesses for obstruction or residual urine
supporting.only_if: recurrent urinary infection or suspected chronic obstruction

not_indicated.why: Not needed unless there is systemic infection or severe cellulitis
Routine metabolic panel does not change management of phimosis
Inflammatory markers are not part of the diagnosis
Rarely changes management; diagnosis is clinical

decision_points: Distinguish phimosis (foreskin cannot be retracted) from paraphimosis (foreskin retracted and stuck behind the glans) — paraphimosis is an emergency
Screen for diabetes in adults with new pathologic phimosis
Consider lichen sclerosus when the foreskin is white, atrophic, or scarred
Urinary retention or systemic infection requires urgent urologic evaluation

differential.name: Paraphimosis
differential.why_considered: Both present with a foreskin that will not move normally and pain at the tip of the penis.
differential.trigger: Foreskin is retracted and stuck behind the glans with a swollen, painful glans

history: Foreskin was retracted and could not be pulled back forward
Often after catheterization, cleaning, or intercourse
exam: Foreskin lies behind the glans as a tight constricting band
Swollen, congested glans distal to the band
Foreskin cannot be reduced forward

differential.name: Balanitis and balanoposthitis
differential.why_considered: Redness, soreness and discharge at the glans and foreskin are common in both, and balanitis often coexists with phimosis.

history: Acute onset of redness, pain and discharge
Often after unprotected intercourse or poor hygiene
exam: Erythema and edema of the glans and foreskin
Purulent or foul-smelling preputial discharge
Foreskin may still be retractable in mild cases
labs: Swab for culture if discharge is present
Glucose or A1c if diabetes suspected

differential.name: Lichen sclerosus of the penis
differential.why_considered: A common cause of pathologic phimosis in adults and children, with scarring that tightens the foreskin.

history: Gradual tightening of the foreskin over months
White, shiny patches on the foreskin or glans
exam: White, atrophic, sclerotic plaques on the foreskin or glans
Loss of normal skin markings
Tight, non-retractile foreskin
labs: Not diagnostic; biopsy if atypical or suspected malignancy

differential.name: Penile cancer
differential.why_considered: Phimosis is a risk factor, and a non-healing ulcer, mass or bleeding under a non-retractile foreskin can be hidden.
differential.trigger: Non-healing penile ulcer, mass, or bleeding in an uncircumcised older man

history: Non-healing sore or growth on the penis
Older age, uncircumcised, HPV or smoking history
exam: Indurated ulcer, nodule or mass on the glans or foreskin
Inguinal lymphadenopathy
Foreskin cannot be retracted to fully inspect the glans
labs: Biopsy of the lesion is diagnostic
imaging: MRI of the penis for local staging if malignancy suspected
Inguinal ultrasound or CT for lymph node assessment

differential.name: Urethral stricture
differential.why_considered: Both can cause a weak urinary stream, straining, and ballooning of the foreskin during voiding.

history: History of urethral trauma, catheterization or sexually transmitted infection
exam: Foreskin may be retractable
Palpable urethral induration or meatal narrowing
Post-void dribbling
imaging: Retrograde urethrogram shows a narrowed urethral segment

differential.name: Physiologic phimosis of infancy and childhood
differential.why_considered: The foreskin is normally non-retractile in infants and young boys and can be mistaken for disease.

history: No pain, no urinary symptoms, no scarring
Often noted by a parent or during routine care
exam: Foreskin is non-retractile but appears normal, without white scarring or erythema
No ballooning or obstruction

differential.name: Concealed penis
differential.why_considered: The penis appears buried in prepubic fat or scarred skin, which can be mistaken for a tight foreskin.

exam: Penile shaft is present but buried under prepubic fat or scar
Foreskin may be retractable once the penis is exposed
No true narrowing of the preputial opening

severity.mild: Physiologic or mild pathologic phimosis: foreskin cannot be fully retracted but there is no pain, no scarring, no urinary symptoms and no infection.
severity.moderate: Symptomatic phimosis with pain on retraction or erection, recurrent balanitis, ballooning of the foreskin during urination, or white scarring of the foreskin.
severity.severe: Phimosis with urinary obstruction (weak stream, straining, incomplete emptying), recurrent urinary tract infection, or severe balanoposthitis requiring treatment.
severity.critical: Phimosis complicated by acute urinary retention, sepsis, or necrotizing infection of the genitalia; this is a urologic emergency.

red_flags.finding: Foreskin retracted and stuck behind the glans with a swollen, painful glans
red_flags.meaning: Paraphimosis, a urologic emergency requiring immediate reduction

red_flags.finding: Acute urinary retention or inability to void
red_flags.meaning: Obstructive complication of phimosis; needs urgent catheterization or urologic intervention

red_flags.finding: Fever, systemic illness, or rapidly spreading erythema and crepitus
red_flags.meaning: Severe infection such as balanoposthitis with sepsis or necrotizing fasciitis

red_flags.finding: Non-healing ulcer, mass, or bleeding under the foreskin
White, atrophic, sclerotic foreskin with progressive tightening
red_flags.meaning: Lichen sclerosus, which can lead to malignancy and often needs surgical treatment

complications.name: Recurrent balanoposthitis
clues: Redness, pain and discharge at the glans and foreskin

complications.name: Urinary tract infection
clues: More common in children and older adults

complications.name: Urinary obstruction with retention
clues: Weak stream, straining, ballooning of the foreskin

complications.name: Penile cancer
clues: Older uncircumcised man with chronic phimosis

complications.name: Paraphimosis
clues: Foreskin retracted and stuck behind the glans

special_populations.differences: Physiologic phimosis is normal; the foreskin is not expected to be retractable. Do not force retraction. Presentation is usually parental concern rather than symptoms.
May present with ballooning during urination, recurrent balanitis, or difficulty with hygiene. Most physiologic phimosis resolves by adolescence; topical steroids may be used when symptomatic.

More likely to have pathologic phimosis from lichen sclerosus, diabetes, or recurrent infection. Higher risk of urinary obstruction and penile cancer; maintain a low threshold for biopsy of suspicious lesions.
Higher risk of recurrent balanoposthitis and more rapid progression due to poor glycemic control and impaired immunity. Screen for and optimize diabetes.

key_questions.question: Can you pull the foreskin back over the head of the penis?
key_questions.looking_for: Foreskin cannot be retracted to reveal the glans; the core defining symptom

key_questions.question: When did this start, and has it been getting tighter over time?
key_questions.looking_for: Present since birth or gradual tightening over months to years; rapid onset over hours suggests paraphimosis instead

key_questions.question: Is the foreskin stuck behind the head of the penis right now?
key_questions.looking_for: Foreskin retracted and trapped behind the glans with a swollen, painful glans — paraphimosis, a urologic emergency

key_questions.question: Does it hurt when you try to pull the skin back or when you have an erection?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain or discomfort with attempted retraction or erection

key_questions.question: Does the skin balloon up or bulge when you urinate?
key_questions.looking_for: Ballooning of the foreskin during voiding, suggesting a tight preputial opening

key_questions.question: Is your urine stream weak, spraying, or hard to start?
key_questions.looking_for: Obstructive voiding symptoms that suggest a complication of phimosis

key_questions.question: Have you had redness, soreness, swelling, or discharge at the tip of the penis?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent balanitis or balanoposthitis, which often coexists with and worsens phimosis

key_questions.question: Have you ever had trouble urinating or been unable to urinate at all?
key_questions.looking_for: Urinary retention, an obstructive complication requiring urgent evaluation

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any white, shiny, or scarred patches on the foreskin?
key_questions.looking_for: Lichen sclerosus, a common cause of pathologic phimosis and a risk factor for malignancy

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, or have you been told your blood sugar is high?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes, a strong risk factor for pathologic phimosis and recurrent infection

key_questions.question: Have you had any trauma, catheterization, or surgery on the penis?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior instrumentation or scarring that could cause a non-retractile foreskin

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any non-healing sore, growth, or bleeding on the penis?
key_questions.looking_for: Possible penile cancer hidden under a non-retractile foreskin, especially in an older uncircumcised man

key_questions.question: Are you circumcised?
key_questions.looking_for: Uncircumcised status; circumcised men are essentially spared unless there is scarring at the circumcision line

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills, or feeling generally unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: Systemic infection such as severe balanoposthitis or sepsis

reasoning_points: The foreskin cannot be retracted to reveal the glans, which is the defining feature of phimosis
Onset is gradual or congenital rather than the sudden onset of paraphimosis
The foreskin is not trapped behind the glans, and there is no constricting band, ruling out paraphimosis
Associated features such as ballooning during urination, weak stream, pain with retraction, or recurrent balanitis support the diagnosis
White, atrophic, or sclerotic foreskin suggests lichen sclerosus as the underlying cause
Diabetes is screened for because it is a strong risk factor for pathologic phimosis and recurrent balanoposthitis
Urinary retention, systemic infection, or a non-healing penile lesion are red flags requiring urgent or urologic evaluation
Physiologic phimosis is normal in infancy and early childhood and usually resolves by adolescence
